questions.q: In the GRC acronym, what does "governance" specifically contribute that risk management and compliance don't?
options: A list of every regulation the organization is subject to
Decision rights and accountability — who can approve a risk acceptance, own a control, or authorize an exception
The evidence auditors collect during a SOC 2 audit
A quantitative estimate of annualized loss expectancy
questions.explain: Governance is about decision rights and accountability: who is authorized to decide, and who answers for the outcome. Risk management assesses and treats risk; compliance meets external/internal obligations.

questions.q: How does the risk management practice from Chapter 3 relate to a GRC program?
options: It is replaced entirely by GRC tooling once a program matures
It only applies before a GRC program exists, not after
It operates independently of GRC and is never coordinated with it
It functions as GRC's risk engine — the identify/assess/treat practice that GRC coordinates alongside governance and compliance
questions.explain: GRC doesn't replace the risk management practice — it coordinates it with governance (decision rights) and compliance (external/internal obligations) so the same controls and decisions aren't tracked three separate times.

questions.q: What real failure mode does treating governance, risk, and compliance as one coordinated program (rather than three silos) prevent?
options: A control owner being asked for the same evidence multiple times, in different formats, by three separate teams assessing the same control independently
The organization having too few documented policies
Internal audit being given too much authority over operational teams
Risk registers becoming too detailed to be useful
questions.explain: Without coordination, three separate teams each map the same real controls to their own framework and request the same evidence separately — more exhausting for control owners, without making anything safer.

questions.q: In the three lines of defense model, what does the second line do that the first line does not?
options: Writes the application code that enforces access control
Configures the firewall rules directly
Sets policy, monitors controls, and independently challenges the first line's own assessment of its risk
Only gets involved after an external audit has already found a problem
questions.explain: The first line is operational management doing the actual work (configuring systems, writing code). The second line is the risk/compliance function setting policy and challenging the first line's self-assessment.

questions.q: What does internal audit, as the third line of defense, verify that the other two lines cannot verify about themselves?
options: Whether the first two lines are actually doing what they claim, independently of both
The exact dollar figure of annualized loss expectancy for every risk
Which specific regulation applies to a new product line
The technical configuration of a single firewall rule
questions.explain: Internal audit is independent of both operational management and the risk/compliance function, so it can verify their claims rather than relying on either line's self-report.
